chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
title: Mancini, Hefti and J.J. Johnson's Across 110th Street
summary: They discuss composers' use of orchestrators, and Kirchner notes J.J. Johnson's percussion cue echoed Mandel's I Want to Live! cue.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Is that, do you think that’s still a pretty common attitude among say composers of your generation who got into film writing like Mancini and Neal Hefti and J.J. Johnson…

I can only speak to myself, Mancini always used an orchestrator but if you looked at his sketches everything was there. I don’t think Neal did a great deal of film. J.J. I don’t know what kind of film J. did, he’s a wonderful writer though and Neal is too.

J.J. got in fairly late in the game I think, in around late 60s, 1970. As a matter of fact I’ll just tell you a quick story. I was at a seminar last week that was given by somebody who's writing J.J.'s biography and he played a film clip from a movie that J.J. had done in the early 70s called, Across 110th Street.
Oh, yeah, yeah, I remember that film.

And there was a percussion segment and it was very similar to the one you did for, I Want to Live! which I pointed out to J.J.'s biography and he was very intrigued by that. It was just, I won’t say it was a copy but it was conceptually very similar to what you did.
Uh-huh, I never heard this score so I…
But if J.J. copied anything I ever did, I’d be highly complimented.
